pl-l3d23c6-d1e115.summary: Affirms, despite the many senses of 'faith', that faith is one, citing Paul: 'one Lord, one faith'.
claims: Faith is one, notwithstanding the several senses of the term.

pl-l3d23c6-d1e124.summary: Explains the unity of faith under both senses: as content believed, it is one because all believers are commanded to believe the same thing, hence it is called catholic or universal; as the means by which one believes, it is one not numerically but in kind, that is, by likeness.
claims: Faith as content is one because all the faithful believe the same thing.
Faith as the means of believing is one in genus (by likeness), not in number.

pl-l3d23c6-d1e127.summary: Supports the point with Augustine: faith is common to all the faithful as a face is common to many people, though each has their own; it is one in kind, not number, called one rather than many because of likeness, as with one will among those who will the same thing.
claims: Each believer has their own faith, which is similar, not identical, to others'.
Faith is called one because of likeness, as a common will or face is.

pl-l3d23c6.summary: Explains in what sense faith is one (Ephesians 4:5) despite the several senses of the word. Faith as the content believed is numerically one and the same for all, hence 'catholic'; faith as the means of believing is one only in kind or by likeness, as Augustine shows with the analogy of a common face or a common will.
claims: Faith is one despite being said in several ways.
As content believed, faith is one and the same for all believers, hence universal (catholic).
As the habit by which one believes, faith is one not in number but in kind, by likeness.
